about.heading: Equitable systems. Resilient land. Enduring human prosperity.
about.lead: Growth Innovation for Development Action (GIDA) is a specialized development organization incorporated as a Company Limited by Guarantee (LTD/GTE) in Kano, Nigeria. We bridge systemic research with pragmatic, community-anchored execution.
about.approach: Our holistic model addresses rural poverty not as isolated technical deficits, but as deeply interconnected market failures, planetary vulnerabilities, and structural social exclusion.

articles.title: International Day of Rural Women 2026, GIDA, Rural Women, Financial Inclusion, Financial Health, Women's Economic Empowerment, Gender-Disaggregated Data, PreCEFI, Rural Development, Nigeria
articles.author: GIDA Communications
articles.excerpt: GIDA commemorated International Day of Rural Women 2026 with a national dialogue bringing together 62 participants to explore how financial inclusion can translate into lasting financial health, economic empowerment and resilience for rural women in Nigeria.
articles.content:
GIDA Commemorates International Day of Rural Women 2026 with National Dialogue on Financial Health
Published by Growth Innovation for Development Action (GIDA) | 15 October 2026

Growth Innovation for Development Action (GIDA) commemorated the 2026 International Day of Rural Women on 15 October with a national virtual dialogue themed “Rural Women Rising: Strengthening the Frontline in Nigeria.” The dialogue focused on moving beyond financial inclusion towards financial health, exploring how rural women can achieve lasting economic security through access to appropriate financial services, resources and opportunities.



The event brought together 62 participants, including development partners, financial service providers, implementing partners and donors from across Nigeria and beyond, to discuss a critical question: How can financial inclusion translate into meaningful improvements in the lives and livelihoods of rural women?
From Financial Inclusion to Financial Health
Although Nigeria has made progress in expanding access to financial services, access alone does not guarantee financial security. According to the EFInA 2026 Access to Financial Services in Nigeria survey cited during the dialogue, 79% of adults are financially included, while 73% are formally included. However, only about 31% of formally included adults are financially healthy, highlighting the need to focus on outcomes beyond account ownership.



For rural women, financial health means having the capacity to manage daily expenses, withstand financial shocks, invest in livelihoods, build assets and plan for the future. It also includes preparing for retirement, accessing health insurance and developing sustainable financial management practices.
The dialogue reinforced GIDA's commitment to ensuring that financial services respond to the realities, needs and aspirations of rural women.
Strengthening Partnerships for Lasting Impact
The keynote address was delivered by Dr Nurudeen Abubakar Zauro, Technical Adviser to the President on Economic and Financial Inclusion and Executive Secretary of the Presidential Committee on Economic and Financial Inclusion (PreCEFI).



Speaking on “Promise or Publicity: PreCEFI as a Leading Institution Bridging Financial Inclusion Gaps,” Dr Zauro emphasised the importance of translating financial inclusion policies into measurable, practical outcomes, particularly at the grassroots level.
He highlighted opportunities for collaboration with organisations working to connect funds to underserved communities, digitise rural value chains, expand agent networks, support national training initiatives and measure meaningful impact.
The dialogue also featured Olajumoke Daramola, Specialist in Advisory Services at Women's World Banking, who introduced the Women's Economic Empowerment (WEE) Barometer. The framework provides a way for financial service providers, donors and development organisations to assess women's empowerment beyond access to financial products.
It examines four dimensions of change: material, cognitive, perceptual and relational. These dimensions help stakeholders understand whether financial interventions are improving women's resources, knowledge, confidence and relationships.



Key Lessons from the Dialogue
The discussions highlighted several priorities for advancing the financial well-being of rural women:
- Measure outcomes, not just access: Financial products and programmes should be assessed by their actual impact on women's lives.
- Strengthen collaboration: Partnerships between government institutions, financial service providers, development organisations and donors are essential for scaling inclusive financial initiatives.
- Design services around rural realities: Financial products must reflect how rural women earn, save, borrow and manage their livelihoods.
- Invest in evidence and accountability: Gender-disaggregated data and practical measurement frameworks can help stakeholders identify gaps and design more effective interventions.
Participants also expressed interest in learning more about PreCEFI and exploring opportunities for collaboration to advance economic and financial inclusion.
GIDA's Commitment to Rural Women's Financial Empowerment
At GIDA, we believe that financial inclusion is not the finish line; financial health is the goal.



Our work focuses on developing approaches that respond to the realities of rural women, including the use of gender-disaggregated data and innovative financing models. Through tools such as CreditHer, which placed third in the Alliance for Innovative Regulation and Central Bank of Nigeria Gender-Disaggregated Data for Impact Design Sprint, and flexible financing approaches such as Buy-Now-Pay-Later and Pay-As-You-Go embedded in village savings structures, GIDA continues to explore ways to make financial services more accessible, relevant and responsive.
We are committed to translating the insights from this dialogue into our programmes and partnerships. Our collaboration with PreCEFI will support efforts to connect funds to the frontline and digitise rural value chains, helping bring financial opportunities closer to the women and communities that need them.


We invite financial institutions, development partners, donors and implementing organisations to join us in advancing practical solutions that strengthen rural women's economic agency and resilience.
Celebrating Rural Women, Strengthening Their Futures
GIDA extends its appreciation to Dr Nurudeen Abubakar Zauro and Olajumoke Daramola for sharing their expertise, to Food Systems Watch (FSW) for partnering with us in commemorating this important day, and to all participants who contributed their insights and perspectives.
Rural women are already building livelihoods, feeding communities and sustaining households. Our collective responsibility is to ensure that financial systems recognise their contributions and provide the support they need to thrive.

When rural women are financially healthy, families and communities are better positioned to build resilient futures.
Growth Innovation for Development Action (GIDA) Where People Prosper.

articles.title: Beyond Gender-Blind Finance: How Gender-Disaggregated Data and Inclusive Innovation Are Transforming Agricultural Finance
articles.author: GIDA Communications
articles.excerpt: True financial inclusion requires more than expanding access to financial services. It requires systems designed around the realities of the people they intend to serve. GIDA explores how gender-disaggregated data, alternative credit assessment, and flexible financing models can improve access to finance for women farmers and agribusiness entrepreneurs.
articles.content:
Financial inclusion is widely recognised as an important driver of poverty reduction and rural economic resilience. Yet, despite the growth of digital financial services across Sub-Saharan Africa, women particularly female smallholder farmers and agribusiness entrepreneurs continue to face significant barriers to accessing finance.
These challenges include limited access to formal land titles and conventional collateral, seasonal cash-flow patterns, mobility constraints and social dynamics that are often overlooked by traditional financial systems. Financial products designed around gender-neutral assumptions can therefore unintentionally exclude the very communities they are intended to support. 


From Assumptions to Evidence:
Gender-disaggregated data provides an opportunity to move financial decision-making from assumptions to evidence. By examining the specific economic behaviours and experiences of women, financial institutions can better understand repayment patterns, seasonal cash flows and structural barriers affecting women-led enterprises.
For example, data from community-based financial systems such as Village Savings and Loan Associations can provide evidence of repayment behaviour that may not appear in conventional credit records. 

This creates opportunities to develop risk-assessment models that better reflect the realities of rural women.

De-Risking Female Agripreneurs Through CreditHer
One practical response to this challenge is CreditHer, an alternative credit-assessment framework co-developed by GIDA's Lead, Inclusive Development, alongside a multidisciplinary team of financial systems, gender and agritech specialists.


The solution was recently recognised with 3rd place at the AIR × CBN Activating Gender-Disaggregated Data for Impact Design Sprint.


CreditHer is designed for female agripreneurs who may lack formal credit histories or fixed collateral. Rather than relying solely on conventional bank records and property ownership, the framework considers alternative indicators such as VSLA transaction records, mobile money history, group savings consistency, social collateral and peer guarantees.

Making Finance More Flexible
Access to credit alone is not enough. The structure of financing also determines whether women can realistically adopt productivity-enhancing technologies.
Flexible financing models such as Buy-Now-Pay-Later (BNPL) and Pay-As-You-Go (PAYG) can reduce the burden of large upfront costs for agricultural technologies and inputs. By aligning payments with harvest and sales cycles, these models can make solutions such as solar-powered irrigation systems, improved seeds and other climate-smart technologies more accessible to female smallholders.     


Building Financial Systems That Work for Everyone
Achieving meaningful financial inclusion requires moving beyond participation toward genuine economic agency.


When gender-disaggregated data informs credit assessment, and flexible financing mechanisms are integrated into local market systems, underserved women can gain stronger pathways into formal finance and productive investment.
At GIDA, we remain committed to working with policymakers, financial institutions, researchers and private-sector partners to develop evidence-driven and market-led solutions that build financial systems capable of reaching every actor across the value chain.

Interested in partnering with GIDA on gender-responsive financial innovation? Connect with our team to explore opportunities for collaboration.

articles.title: Scaling Regenerative Soil Systems Across Northern Agricultural Corridors
articles.author: GIDA Agronomy Team
articles.excerpt: How bio-innovations, indigenous compost amendments, and microbial soil testing are revitalizing exhausted farmlands while raising smallholder yields by over 38%.
articles.content:
Sustainable rural prosperity starts with the health of the soil under our feet. For generations, northern farming clusters have battled severe topsoil degradation, nutrient leaching, and dependency on costly synthetic inputs that degrade long-term soil biology.

Over the past two cropping seasons, GIDA's Community & Planetary Health team has partnered with over 12,000 smallholders across Kano, Jigawa, and Kaduna corridors to pilot low-cost bio-safe soil fertility protocols.

### The Core Interventions

1. **On-Farm Microbial Soil Testing:** Rapid colorimetric assays enabling farmers to assess nitrogen, phosphorus, and organic carbon levels within minutes at the farm gate.
2. **Indigenous Microorganism (IMO) Culturing:** Sourcing indigenous forest fungi and beneficial microbes to accelerate organic compost fermentation from 90 days down to 21 days.
3. **Cover Crop Nitrogen Fixation:** Integrating deep-rooted leguminous cover crops into cereal rotations, sequestering atmospheric nitrogen while suppressing weed proliferation without herbicides.

### Documented Field Impact

Initial harvest data demonstrates that participating farmer clusters achieved a 38.4% increase in sorghum and millet yields, alongside a 45% reduction in synthetic fertilizer expenditure. Furthermore, soil moisture retention increased measurably, shielding crops during dry spells and late-season heatwaves.

As we expand this model to 50,000 farmers in 2027, GIDA remains committed to transforming scientific ecological research into practical, community-owned wealth.

articles.title: Women-Led Solar Cold Hubs: Breaking the Post-Harvest Loss Cycle
articles.author: Amina Bello, Market Systems Lead
articles.excerpt: Deploying 100% solar-powered decentralized cold storage units managed exclusively by female cooperative clusters in rural aggregation centers.
articles.content:
In horticultural value chains across northern Nigeria, post-harvest losses among perishable crops such as tomatoes, peppers, and leafy greens routinely exceed 42%. Smallholder women, who bear the primary burden of harvest aggregation and retail trading, are forced to distress-sell at cut-throat prices before evening sets in.

GIDA's Green Infrastructure and GESI units joined forces to introduce decentralized, solar-powered walk-in cold rooms located directly at key rural trading junctions.

### Cooperative Ownership & Governance

Unlike conventional top-down donor projects, these facilities are structured as community-owned enterprises governed entirely by female agricultural cooperatives:

- **Pay-As-You-Store Micro-Fees:** Farmers pay a modest daily crate fee (less than 10% of typical distress-sale losses), ensuring commercial viability and ongoing maintenance reserves.
- **Digital Traceability & Inventory:** A simplified Hausa-language mobile SMS ledger tracks crate ownership, temperature stability, and release times.
- **Direct Institutional Off-Taking:** Aggregated produce meets institutional buyer standards, allowing women to sell directly to urban supermarkets and processors at premium rates.

### Results and Next Phase

Participating cooperatives recorded an 85% reduction in spoilage and a 52% average increase in seasonal household income. GIDA is now structuring blended micro-guarantee facilities with regional financial institutions to deploy 30 additional units across regional agricultural corridors.

articles.title: One Health at the Frontline: Surveillance of Zoonotic Pathogens in Livestock Corridors
articles.author: Dr. Kabir Sani, Epidemiologist
articles.excerpt: Bridging veterinary medicine, human clinical care, and ecological monitoring to safeguard rural communities against emerging infectious spillover risks.
articles.content:
The boundary between human well-being, livestock resilience, and ecological stability is inseparable. In pastoral and agro-pastoral communities, close daily contact between animals and families creates critical vulnerabilities to zoonotic transmissions and antimicrobial resistance.

GIDA's One Health initiative unites local veterinary officers, primary healthcare workers, and pastoralist leaders in a coordinated early-warning sentinel surveillance network.

### Integrated Community Health Protocols

- **Cross-Sectoral Diagnostic Teams:** Joint health post visits where veterinary and human clinicians share syndromic reports, tracking fever clusters and livestock abortions concurrently.
- **Antimicrobial Stewardship:** Discouraging prophylactic antibiotic misuse in cattle and poultry through participatory community dialogues and subsidized probiotic alternatives.
- **Clean Water Point Separation:** Engineering bio-sand filtration systems that physically isolate human domestic drinking points from livestock watering troughs.

By building trusted institutional connections between pastoralists and public health authorities, GIDA is demonstrating that planetary health is fundamental to rural security and economic dignity.

vacancies.title: Senior Rural Market Systems Specialist
vacancies.summary: Lead the co-design and execution of inclusive market linkages, digital financial tools, and equitable value-chain partnerships for smallholders and NMSMEs.
responsibilities: Design and execute MSD (Market Systems Development) strategies tailored to northern agricultural corridors.
Structure commercial partnerships between smallholder farmer clusters, bio-input suppliers, and institutional off-takers.
Supervise field assessments on post-harvest aggregation, cold-chain logistics, and digital traceability systems.
Co-create catalytic de-risking mechanisms, including blended finance tools and micro-guarantee facilities for female agri-entrepreneurs.
Conduct periodic market analyses, price monitoring, and regulatory reviews affecting smallholder market participation.
qualifications: Master's degree in Agricultural Economics, Agribusiness Management, Development Finance, or related field.
6–8 years of demonstrated experience implementing donor-funded (FCDO, USAID, World Bank, AGRA) MSD market programs.
Deep knowledge of northern Nigerian rural economies and cooperative governance structures.

vacancies.title: One Health & Bio-Innovations Officer
vacancies.summary: Spearhead microbial water testing, mycotoxin post-harvest mitigation, and bio-safe soil fertility protocols across rural cluster cooperatives.
responsibilities: Implement field-level microbiological water quality and aflatoxin screening assays.
Deliver bio-pesticide, organic composting, and soil remediation training to cluster cooperatives.
Manage zoonotic surveillance protocols in collaboration with local veterinary and public health departments.
Document environmental indicator benchmarks for the GIDA Planetary Health repository.
qualifications: Degree in Microbiology, Environmental Health, Agronomy, Veterinary Medicine, or Biochemistry.
3–5 years of laboratory and field testing experience in rural agricultural environments.
Hands-on expertise with rapid bio-assay kits and environmental health auditing tools.

vacancies.title: GESI & Safeguarding Focal Lead
vacancies.summary: Oversee community-based grievance redress mechanisms, PSEAH compliance standards, and transformative gender empowerment across all operations.
responsibilities: Manage confidential reporting channels and grievance redress mechanisms across all project hubs.
Conduct comprehensive safeguarding onboarding and training for staff, contractors, and partner organizations.
Ensure gender-transformative indicators and safe space mechanisms are embedded in all project lifecycles.
Lead incident triage in strict accordance with the 24-hour / 48-hour mandatory escalation timeline.
qualifications: Degree in Social Work, Human Rights, International Law, Gender Studies, or Development Studies.
5+ years managing safeguarding, protection, or PSEAH systems in complex rural contexts.
Demonstrated confidentiality, emotional intelligence, and crisis management expertise.
